Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Causes small, water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves that enlarge and turn brown, leading to premature leaf drop and fruit spotting.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and resistant pepper cultivars.
Apply fixed copper-based bactericides at the earliest sign of infection.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; water at the base of the plant.
Sanitize pruning tools and rotate crops away from solanaceous plants for at least 2 years.

Pepper__bell___healthy.description: Leaf exhibits deep green color, smooth foliage, intact margins, and no visible spots or chlorosis.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture without waterlogging.
Apply balanced N-P-K fertilizer and ensure adequate calcium to prevent blossom end rot.
Inspect leaves weekly for early signs of aphids or thrips.
Ensure 6 to 8 hours of daily direct sunlight.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Characterized by dark brown to black circular lesions on older leaves, often displaying a classic concentric 'target board' or bullseye ring pattern.
prevention: Apply preventative fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper compounds.
Ensure proper plant spacing for air circulation to accelerate leaf drying.
Avoid overhead irrigation and irrigate in early morning.
Practice 3-year crop rotation and eradicate solanaceous weeds (nightshade).

Potato___Late_blight.description: Highly destructive water mold causing large, irregular water-soaked dark lesions with pale green halos, often with white fungal fuzz on leaf undersides in high humidity.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers; destroy cull piles before planting.
Apply protective fungicides (e.g., cymoxanil, dimethomorph, or copper) before cool, wet weather.
Promptly remove and destroy infected vines to prevent spores from washing into soil tubers.
Allow at least 2 weeks after vine death before harvesting tubers to minimize skin inoculation.

Potato___healthy.description: Leaflets show vibrant green coloration, firm texture, well-defined veins, and no necrotic lesions or mildew.
prevention: Hill soil regularly around stems to protect growing tubers from greening and pests.
Maintain even soil moisture throughout the tuber initiation and bulking stages.
Scout fields twice a week during rainy or humid spells.
Apply balanced potassium and nitrogen fertilizers as recommended by soil tests.

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.description: Manifests as small, greasy, dark brown angular lesions on leaves, often surrounded by yellow halos. Leaves may turn yellow, scorch, and drop.
prevention: Treat seeds with hot water or buy certified disease-free seedlings.
Spray copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb for improved efficacy.
Do not work in tomato patches when foliage is wet.
Rotate fields with non-host crops (corn, beans) for at least 2 consecutive seasons.

Tomato_Early_blight.description: Produces brown-black spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first, spreading upwards with extensive yellowing around the spots.
prevention: Mulch soil around plants to prevent soil-borne fungal spores from splashing onto foliage.
Prune the lowest leaves (bottom 12 inches) once plants are established to maximize airflow.
Apply copper fungicide or biofungicide (Bacillus subtilis) preventively.
Disinfect cages and stakes at the end of each growing season.

Tomato_Late_blight.description: Rapidly spreading greasy dark gray-brown patches on leaves and stems. Under humid conditions, white spore growth appears on the leaf undersides.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant PHR, Plum Regal).
Avoid overhead watering; use drip lines or soaker hoses.
Apply preventive fungicides prior to cool, rainy forecasts.
Immediately bag and remove severely infected plants; do not compost them.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.description: Pale yellow patches appear on upper leaf surfaces while olive-green to velvet brown fungal spores develop directly beneath on the undersides.
prevention: Reduce relative humidity inside greenhouses below 85% with adequate ventilation.
Increase plant spacing and prune suckers to promote air circulation.
Avoid wetting the foliage during watering.
Apply protective sulfur or copper fungicides when high humidity is sustained.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Numerous small circular spots (1/8 inch) with dark brown margins and sunken grayish-white centers dotted with tiny black pycnidia (spore bodies).
prevention: Remove diseased bottom leaves promptly to prevent the fungus from climbing.
Apply organic straw or plastic mulch to block soil splashing.
Spray chlorothalonil, copper, or potassium bicarbonate at first symptom appearance.
Rotate crops every 2-3 years away from solanaceous plants.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.description: Tiny yellow or white speckling (stippling) on leaves, accompanied by fine silky webbing on leaf undersides. Severe infestations cause leaves to bronze and dry up.
prevention: Spray insecticidal soap, horticultural neem oil, or sulfur on both sides of leaves.
Introduce beneficial predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) in controlled environments.
Maintain adequate soil hydration, as drought and dusty conditions accelerate mite reproduction.
Knock down populations with strong water sprays directed at the undersides of leaves.

Tomato__Target_Spot.description: Pinpoint brown specks that expand into circular brown lesions with distinct concentric target rings and yellow halos.
prevention: Keep plant canopies well pruned to encourage rapid drying after rains.
Ensure proper row orientation relative to prevailing winds.
Apply preventive fungicides labeled for Corynespora (e.g., azoxystrobin or mancozeb).
Destroy plant debris immediately after the final harvest.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.description: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaflets, marked yellowing (chlorosis) of margins, stunted bushy growth, and failure to set fruit.
prevention: Control the primary insect vector: whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) using yellow sticky traps and insecticidal sprays.
Use ultra-fine insect netting in nursery beds and greenhouses.
Plant TYLCV-resistant hybrids (such as Tycoon, Charger, or Red Snapper).
Remove and seal infected plants in plastic bags immediately upon detection.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on foliage, distorted 'shoestring' or fern-like leaf shapes, and reduced plant vigor.
prevention: Wash hands thoroughly with soap or milk solution before handling plants (especially if using tobacco products).
Disinfect garden tools in a 10% household bleach solution between plants.
Select resistant tomato cultivars bearing the 'ToMV' or 'Tm-2' resistance gene.
Do not save seeds from infected plants; eradicate infected specimens without touching healthy neighbors.

Tomato_healthy.description: Vigorous, rich green leaves with crisp margins and clean surfaces, indicating optimal photosynthetically active tissue.
prevention: Water regularly at ground level to provide 1 to 2 inches of moisture per week.
Provide sturdy stakes or trellises to keep foliage off the ground.
Fertilize with phosphorus and potassium once flowering begins to promote sturdy fruit development.
Perform weekly inspections of lower foliage for early disease detection.
